description:
🌌 Nebula Voyagers

We are a team of five young explorers passionate about space, science, technology, and innovation. With interests spanning astronomy, coding, research, AI, and creative problem-solving, we came together to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge and turn our ideas into meaningful solutions.
summary: Icarus Field Manual plans a short human stay at Jezero Crater one sol at a time. For a two-person crew over ten sols it tracks water, oxygen and food, the local solar clock and sunlight, the light delay to Earth, and one hard check for each planned walk: can the crew turn round and get back on suit oxygen with a reserve? Every number carries a tag (live, frozen, computed, cited, scenario assumption, user input or stub), and clicking it opens the source: NASA's Life Support BVAD, the Mars24 algorithm, JPL Horizons, NOAA, and a USGS CTX elevation model. What we have not built shows as "stub", not as a guess. No language model produced any number. This is a v0 prototype, not for mission use.
details: The problem. The first days on Mars come down to bookkeeping: what is left, when it is light, and how far you can go and still return. Planning numbers are often shown without their source or their assumptions. What we built. A v0 vertical slice for Jezero Crater: a Mars clock (Mars Sol Date, season Ls, local noon, EVA window), a supply ledger, a walkback check, a top-of-atmosphere sunlight curve, Earth light-time, a space-weather panel, 11 labelled warnings, and a USGS shaded-relief map of Jezero. How it works. The Icarus Engine (v0.2) does the physics. Supply rates come from NASA's BVAD (Tables 3-31 and 4-70), scaled by 1.027491 days per sol. For the crew, with 2 EVA hours, that gives 7.571 kg of water, 2.183 kg of oxygen and 1.644 kg of food per sol. The walkback check works like this: 2.60 h of suit oxygen, minus a 30% reserve, leaves 1.82 h. At 2.5 km/h that is a 2.27 km walkback radius, so a planned 1.2 km one-way walk passes. Sunlight at local noon is 519 W/m² at 1.6095 AU, with no dust and no atmosphere. The Earth link is 10.90 minutes one way, from JPL Horizons. What makes it different. Every value has one of eight tags and a source behind it. Elevation comes from a frozen, hashed record, JR-001: −2570.22 m, one 20 m cell of the USGS CTX DEM near the Octavia E. Butler landing point. It replaces an earlier QGIS value of −2579.1118 m, and the 8.89 m difference is documented, not hidden. How it addresses the challenge. The challenge asks for a layered, integrated view of a location that helps a human explorer plan a Marswalk. Icarus Field Manual does this for Jezero Crater by combining sources from several NASA programmes in one sol-by-sol view: a USGS/JPL CTX elevation model, NASA supply and suit references, the NASA GISS Mars clock, JPL Horizons for Earth link timing, and NOAA space weather. For each planned walk it checks whether the crew could turn round and get back on suit oxygen. Our map is a rendered relief image with the landing-point marker, not an interactive layered map, and slope is not yet part of the walkback check. We state both gaps openly. Tools. The Icarus Engine (v0.2) for the physics and an Environment Feed (feed.py) that retrieves JPL and NOAA data; the web interface is hosted on Netlify. QGIS was used for an earlier elevation check. Implemented vs missing. Built: the clock, supply ledger, walkback check, sunlight curve, Earth link, space-weather feed, relief map and the frozen record. Not built (shown as STUB): solar array and battery, dust optical depth, air recycling, relay windows, Mars Climate Database, radiation dose and failure modelling. Limits. Not for mission use. The 20 m cell is not a surveyed elevation and not for rock hazards. The suit-oxygen time is a planning assumption, not a sourced Mars suit capacity. Space-weather values are a snapshot from 14 Nov 2026. The check is not a safety guarantee. Next. A dust scenario feeding derated solar output and battery state through the night, then slope-aware walkback and an interactive layered map. Use of SI. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help draft and edit this description, the project summary and the slide deck, and to cross-check arithmetic. No SI model produced any number shown in the prototype. No SI-generated images are used; the relief map is rendered by the Icarus Engine from the USGS CTX DEM.
